title: The ISRO Chief Who Led India to Mars and Never Stopped Dancing Kathakali
excerpt: Dr. K. Radhakrishnan steered Mangalyaan to Mars on India's first attempt while maintaining a parallel life as a Kathakali performer and Carnatic vocalist.
body:
• Dr. K. Radhakrishnan, ISRO Chairman from 2009 to 2014, led India's Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) — making India the first country to reach Mars on its maiden attempt
  • A trained Kathakali performer and Carnatic vocalist, Radhakrishnan has performed at major music festivals across India, including the Guruvayoor Chembai Sangeetholsavam every year since 2008
  • Born in Irinjalakuda, Kerala, he grew up surrounded by performing arts traditions alongside rigorous scientific training — a duality he maintained throughout his career
  • He received the Padma Bhushan in 2014 and was named one of Nature journal's ten people who mattered that year

The Scientist Who Never Left the Stage

In September 2014, when India's Mars Orbiter Mission entered Mars orbit on its very first attempt, the world's attention turned to the man who had steered the mission from conception to execution. Dr. Koppillil Radhakrishnan, then Chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation, had just delivered one of the most cost-effective interplanetary missions in history — achieved for roughly $74 million, less than the budget of many Hollywood films.

What most headlines missed was that the man behind Mangalyaan was also a Kathakali dancer and Carnatic vocalist who had been performing alongside professionals for decades.

Roots in Kerala's Arts Country

Radhakrishnan was born on August 29, 1949, in Irinjalakuda, a small town in Kerala's Thrissur district renowned for its performing arts heritage. The town is home to the Koodalmanikyam temple, one of Kerala's most important cultural institutions, and the arts were as much a part of daily life as academics.

As a young student, Radhakrishnan trained in Kerala Natanam under Professor Thrippunithura Vijayabhanu before progressing to Kathakali under Guru Pallippuram Gopalan Nair, Kalanilayam Raghavan, and T.V.A. Varier. Simultaneously, he studied electrical engineering, graduating from the Government Engineering College, Thrissur in 1970.

"In space, we should not worry about success or failure. The difference between success and failure is very, very thin. But do the job well and do the best."

— Dr. K. Radhakrishnan

Four Decades at ISRO

Radhakrishnan joined ISRO in 1971 at what is now the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in Thiruvananthapuram, working initially as a design engineer on electro-mechanical devices. Over the next four decades, his career spanned avionics systems, remote sensing, satellite launches, and ocean observation.

Between 1974 and 1976, while working at ISRO, he completed a management degree at IIM Bangalore — and began formal training in Carnatic music. It was during this period that he studied under eminent musicians including Prof. Vechoor Harihara Subramania Iyer and Dr. R.K. Srikantan.

In 2000, he became the founding director of the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS). After the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in December 2004, Radhakrishnan led the effort to establish India's tsunami early warning system — a contribution that has since saved thousands of lives across the region.

The Mars Mission

Appointed ISRO Chairman in October 2009, Radhakrishnan oversaw 37 space missions during his five-year tenure. The crown jewel was the Mars Orbiter Mission, conceived, planned, and executed within four years.

Mangalyaan launched on November 5, 2013, from Sriharikota and entered Mars orbit on September 24, 2014, after a 300-day, 670-million-kilometer journey. India became the first country to succeed in reaching Mars on its first attempt, and the mission cost a fraction of comparable American and European efforts.

The achievement earned Radhakrishnan the Padma Bhushan, India's third-highest civilian honor, in 2014. That same year, the journal Nature named him one of its ten people who mattered globally.

Art as Parallel Life

Throughout his tenure at the helm of India's space program, Radhakrishnan never stopped performing. He gave his first public Carnatic music recital at the Koodalmanikyam temple in his hometown in 1980, and has sung at the Guruvayoor Chembai Sangeetholsavam every year since 2008.

His performance venues read like a who's who of South Indian classical music: the Bengaluru Sangeethotsav, the Sankranthi Music Festival, the Chembai Vaidyanatha Bhagavathar Music Festival in Chennai, and the JSS Sangeetha Sabha. In Kathakali, photographs from the 1980s show him in full costume, enacting the role of King Daksha.

His autobiography, My Odyssey: Memoirs of the Man Behind the Mangalyaan Mission, published by Penguin Random House India in 2016, devotes significant space to his artistic life alongside his scientific career.

A Lesson in Not Choosing

Radhakrishnan's story resonates particularly with the Indian diaspora, where the pressure to choose between passions — arts versus STEM, tradition versus modernity — runs deep. Here was a man who led a space agency and performed Kathakali, who managed rocket launches and sang ragas, who earned a doctorate from IIT Kharagpur and trained under classical music masters.

Now 77, Radhakrishnan continues to serve as Chairman of the Board of Governors at IIT Kanpur and IIT Ropar, and remains an Honorary Distinguished Advisor at ISRO. He still performs.
nri_angle: Radhakrishnan's story challenges the arts-vs-STEM binary familiar to diaspora families, showing a life where both passions thrived.
